claims.text: The comparison applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys with X equal to Al, Si, or Mn in single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
CrFeCoNi without an X addition is the baseline for the comparison.
Al-containing CrFeCoNiX will form a slower-growing oxide scale than the Si- and Mn-containing variants above 900 °C.
The oxide scale on the Al-containing alloy will be more coherent and adherent and will exhibit less cracking or spallation than scales on the Si- and Mn-containing alloys.
Al reduces oxygen diffusivity or oxygen ingress in CrFeCoNiX.
Al mitigates interfacial stress accumulation in the oxide scale.
Al favors formation of Al2O3 or mixed Cr-Al oxides.
The Al-containing oxide is a low-strain oxide.
Si and Mn increase oxygen permeability in CrFeCoNiX.
Si- and Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys develop faster-growing, heterogeneous oxide scales.
Growth-induced stresses at an oxide-metal interface can cause scale cracking, spallation, and breakaway oxidation.
Temperature and alloying additions can govern selective oxidation by changing oxygen permeability, solute diffusivity, and transient-oxide growth rate.
Protective-scale behavior is governed by a balance between the chemical driving force for oxide formation and mechanical integrity at the oxide-alloy interface.
Oxide thermodynamics alone do not determine high-temperature oxidation behavior because diffusion, nucleation, and surface-reaction kinetics also affect oxide formation and growth.
The CrFeCoNi baseline lacks the diffusional and stress-modulating effects attributed to Al, Si, and Mn.
The proposed comparison holds base composition and processing conditions constant while changing X among Al, Si, and Mn.
The proposed test uses isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C for 24 hours in a controlled oxidative atmosphere.
Failure of the Al-containing alloy to show significantly slower growth and better scale integrity than both Si- and Mn-containing variants would falsify the hypothesis.
